curatorBrief.title: Welcome to the World of Addition!
curatorBrief.intent: Welcome Kindergarten mathematicians to the magical world of adding! In this lesson, we will explore combining groups of fun objects, learn about our special math symbols the plus sign (+) and equal sign (=), and discover how joining things together makes an even bigger group.

objectiveBlocks.objectiveText: Combine two groups of physical objects to find the total amount

components.title: Adding at the Park
components.intent: Guide kindergarteners to act out joining stories (e.g., 2 ducks joined by 1 duck) by manipulating objects on screen and counting the combined total within 5.

components.title: Fill the Frame
components.intent: Use a single 10-frame to place counters for two distinct groups (e.g., 3 red counters and 2 blue counters) to see and speak the combined sum.

components.title: Roll and Add
components.intent: Practice rolling two dice, counting pip patterns together to find the combined total, and saying the sum out loud to the live tutor.

objectiveBlocks.objectiveText: Identify the plus sign (+) and equal sign (=) as math symbols

components.title: Meet Our Math Symbols
components.intent: Introduce the plus sign (+) as the symbol that puts things together and the equal sign (=) as the symbol that shows the total amount, with clear visual definitions and simple taps.

components.title: Building with Symbols
components.intent: Provide scaffolded hands-on practice dragging the plus sign (+) between two groups and the equal sign (=) before the total to complete basic kindergarten number sentences within 5.

components.title: Name the Symbol
components.intent: Show an isolated math symbol (+ or =) and have the child say 'plus' or 'equals' out loud into the microphone for immediate tutor feedback.

objectiveBlocks.objectiveText: Explain how putting things together makes a bigger number

components.title: Before and After Adding
components.intent: Visually compare a starting group (e.g., 2 apples) with the final group after more are added (e.g., 4 apples) to illustrate that joining makes a bigger group.

components.title: Hopping Forward to Bigger Numbers
components.intent: Use an interactive 0-10 number line with animated jumps to the right, showing that adding more hops moves us forward toward bigger numbers.

components.title: Say the Total
components.intent: Present basic addition facts within 5 and have the child speak the sum, observing that the resulting number is greater than either addend.

finalAssessment.title: Addition Celebration!
finalAssessment.intent: Assess kindergarten understanding across all three objectives: joining two concrete groups, identifying the plus and equal signs, and recognizing that adding makes a larger total.

data.title: Math Symbol Fun
data.description: Say the name of the math symbol you see on the screen out loud.
data.gradeLevel: kindergarten students (ages 5-6) - Use clear language, relatable examples, foundational skills, and engaging visuals. Encourage exploration and basic problem-solving.

items.ask: Look at this math sign. What is the name of this sign?
items.howToPlay: I will show you a word, and you read it out loud.
items.acceptRule: Saying the word with a very soft or stretched starting sound counts as saying the word.
items.signatureError: Saying addition or add instead of the exact name of the sign is not the correct name.
items.correctionBody: This sign is plus. We use plus when we put groups together.

items.ask: Here is another math sign. What do we call this symbol?
items.howToPlay: I will show you a word, and you read it out loud.
items.acceptRule: A child saying just the core word clearly counts as the correct answer.
items.signatureError: Saying and instead of the math term is not the correct name.
items.correctionBody: This is the plus sign. It means we are adding more.

items.ask: Check out this symbol on the screen. What is its name?
items.howToPlay: I will show you a word, and you read it out loud.
items.acceptRule: Stating the symbol name loudly and clearly counts as the correct answer.
items.signatureError: Saying cross instead of the math term sounds similar but is not the right name.
items.correctionBody: The name of this symbol is plus. It tells us to join numbers.

items.ask: Tell me the name of this math symbol right here.
items.howToPlay: I will show you a word, and you read it out loud.
items.acceptRule: Pronouncing the word with a little excitement still counts as the correct answer.
items.signatureError: Saying positive instead of the math sign is not the right word.
items.correctionBody: This sign is plus. It helps us put things together in math.

data.title: Making Groups Bigger
data.intro: Watch how putting things together makes more!

item1.name: Start Group
item1.description: Two yummy red apples sitting on the table.
item1.visualPrompt: A cute drawing of two red apples in a row, bright colors, simple style for kindergarten

item2.name: Add More
item2.description: Four yummy red apples together now.
item2.visualPrompt: A cute drawing of four red apples grouped together, bright colors, simple style for kindergarten

synthesis.mainInsight: Putting apples together makes a bigger group of apples.
synthesis.commonMisconception: Thinking the number stays the same when you put more together.

whenToUse.item1Context: Use the start group when you have your very first toys.
whenToUse.item2Context: Use the add more group when you get more toys.

gates.question: The start group has two apples.
gates.rationale: Great job! The start group shows two apples before we add any more.

gates.question: Putting groups together makes a smaller number.
gates.rationale: Not quite! Putting groups together always makes a bigger number, just like four is bigger than two.

data.title: Hop Along the Number Line

challenges.instruction: Put your frog on the number 7. Hop backward 1 space to the left!
challenges.hint: Count just 1 single hop backward to see where you land.

challenges.hint: Start your finger on 2 and count 2 hops backward to the left.

challenges.instruction: Put your finger on the number 3. Make a big jump forward of 2 spaces to the right!
challenges.hint: Count 2 hops to the right from the number 3 to see where you land.

challenges.instruction: Put your finger on the number 5, and then hop back 2 spaces to the left!
challenges.hint: Count out loud as you take your 2 hops backward!

data.title: Fun Addition Practice!
data.description: Let us look at some addition problems and say the answers out loud together.
data.gradeLevel: kindergarten students (ages 5-6) - Use clear language, relatable examples, foundational skills, and engaging visuals. Encourage exploration and basic problem-solving.

problems.question: Two apples and one more apple make how many?
problems.rationale: When you start with 2 apples and add 1 more, you count forward one to get 3 apples. Putting groups together is called addition, so 2 plus 1 equals 3. Practicing counting objects one by one helps us find the total amount.
problems.teachingNote: Encourage students to use concrete manipulatives or their fingers to count on from 2 when adding 1.
successCriteria: Add two small groups of objects within five to find the total sum
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.statement: The plus sign (+) means we take away objects.
problems.rationale: The plus sign actually means we put things together to make more, not take them away. When we see a plus sign, we are adding objects to a group. Taking away objects is what the minus sign (-) does.
problems.teachingNote: Kindergarten students often confuse the plus sign with the minus sign because both involve math symbols. Use physical counters to show that plus adds more items, while minus removes them.
successCriteria: Recognize the meaning of the plus sign (+) in addition
Distinguish between addition and subtraction actions
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: What happens when we put two groups of toys together?
problems.rationale: When we use addition to join groups together, we get more in total. Putting two sets of toys into one pile makes the number of toys get bigger. That is why combining groups means the count increases!
problems.teachingNote: Reinforce the core concept of addition as combining or joining sets. Use physical manipulatives like counting bears or blocks so students can visibly watch the pile grow larger.
successCriteria: Identify that joining two groups increases the total amount
Understand the basic concept of addition as making a group bigger

inset.definition: Putting groups together to make a bigger number.
inset.exampleSentence: When we use addition with our blocks, the tower gets taller.
inset.label: Word Helper

problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: Two stars and two stars make how many stars?
problems.rationale: When you have two stars and join two more stars, you count them all together: one, two, three, four. Adding two and two makes a total of four stars. Counting all the stars together gives the correct sum.
problems.teachingNote: Have students use counters or fingers to model the two groups before joining them together and counting the total.
successCriteria: Model addition by putting two sets of objects together.
Find the sum of two sets up to five.

detectedConstraints.description: The equal sign (=) is omitted from all symbol identification items in obj2-symbol-spotter and final assessment.
obj3-number-line-hops focuses predominantly on backward subtraction jumps rather than demonstrating that addition results in a larger number.
obj3-math-facts-fluency tests basic arithmetic fact retrieval rather than explaining or demonstrating why combining groups yields a bigger number.

coverage.summary: The lesson strongly teaches and assesses combining concrete sets (Objective 1) using multiple interactive representations. However, Objective 2 assesses only the plus sign while completely omitting identification of the equal sign, and Objective 3 relies on off-target computation and subtraction blocks, leaving only a single multiple-choice question to assess the concept that addition makes numbers bigger.
